articles.title: Goodbye, cavities? Scientists create gel that could regrow tooth enamel
articles.summary: Scientists have developed a revolutionary gel that could regrow lost tooth enamel by harnessing minerals naturally found in saliva, potentially overcoming one of dentistry’s biggest limitations. The regenerated enamel behaves much like healthy enamel, raising hopes for a simple treatment that could repair damaged teeth, prevent decay, and reduce sensitivity.
articles.content:
Scientists have developed a new gel that could make it possible to regrow damaged tooth enamel, potentially overcoming one of the biggest limitations in dental care. Unlike bones and many other tissues in the body, tooth enamel cannot naturally regenerate once it has been lost. The new treatment offers a promising way to rebuild this protective layer, strengthen teeth, and help prevent future decay.

The innovation comes from researchers at the University of Nottingham's School of Pharmacy and Department of Chemical and Environmental Engineering. Their new material is inspired by the biological processes that form tooth enamel during early childhood. It is designed to repair enamel that has been weakened by mineral loss or worn away by erosion, while also reinforcing enamel that remains healthy.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, could pave the way for a new generation of dental treatments that go beyond protecting existing enamel and actually help restore its structure.

How the New Gel Regrows Tooth Enamel

One of the most promising features of the technology is its simplicity. Dentists could apply the gel directly to teeth using a procedure similar to existing fluoride treatments, making it potentially easy to incorporate into routine dental care.

Unlike conventional fluoride products, however, the new gel contains no fluoride. Instead, it uses a material made from proteins that imitates important characteristics of the natural proteins responsible for guiding enamel formation when teeth first develop.

Once applied, the gel forms a thin but durable coating that penetrates the tooth's surface and fills microscopic cracks and gaps. This coating then provides a framework for rebuilding the mineral structure of enamel.

The process relies on calcium and phosphate ions, two essential mineral components naturally present in saliva. The gel attracts these minerals and helps organize them into new crystals that grow in an orderly pattern.

Scientists call this process epitaxial mineralization. Essentially, it means that new mineral crystals grow in alignment with the existing enamel, allowing the newly formed material to become structurally integrated with the original tooth surface.

This organization is especially important because enamel gets its exceptional hardness and durability from the precise arrangement of its mineral crystals. Simply depositing minerals on a tooth is not enough to recreate the complex structure that makes natural enamel so effective.

By guiding crystal growth, the new gel can restore both the microscopic architecture and the physical properties of healthy enamel.

A Potential Solution for Tooth Sensitivity and Decay

The researchers also discovered that their material can be used on exposed dentine, commonly called dentin in the United States. Dentin is the layer of tooth tissue beneath the enamel. It is softer than enamel and contains tiny channels that can transmit sensations toward the nerves inside the tooth.

When enamel wears away, or gums recede, exposed dentin can make teeth particularly sensitive to hot, cold, sweet, or acidic foods and drinks.

The new gel can encourage the formation of an enamel-like mineral layer over exposed dentin. This could help reduce tooth sensitivity while also improving the attachment of dental restorations, such as fillings and other treatments used to repair damaged teeth.

The potential benefits are significant. Enamel deterioration is a major factor in tooth decay and contributes to dental problems that affect nearly half of the world's population. These conditions can cause pain, infections, and eventually tooth loss. Poor oral health is also associated with broader health problems, including diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

One of the greatest challenges in dentistry is that enamel has no living cells capable of rebuilding it after teeth have fully developed. Although saliva can naturally replace some minerals lost during the earliest stages of enamel damage, the body cannot regenerate substantial amounts of enamel that have been worn away.

Existing treatments, including fluoride varnishes and remineralization products, can help protect teeth and repair early mineral loss. However, they cannot fully reconstruct enamel that has already been lost.

The new technology aims to overcome that limitation by encouraging the formation of new mineral tissue with properties resembling those of the original enamel.

Regenerated Enamel Performs Like Natural Tooth Enamel

The research team tested the mechanical strength and durability of the regenerated material under conditions designed to mimic everyday use.

These experiments examined how the newly formed enamel responded to activities and exposures that teeth routinely experience, including brushing, chewing, and contact with acidic foods.

The results were encouraging. According to the researchers, the regenerated enamel displayed mechanical properties comparable to those of healthy natural enamel, suggesting that the material could provide more than a temporary protective coating.

Dr. Abshar Hasan, a postdoctoral fellow and the study's lead author, explained why recreating enamel's internal structure is so important.

"Dental enamel has a unique structure, which gives enamel its remarkable properties that protect our teeth throughout life against physical, chemical, and thermal insults. When our material is applied to demineralized or eroded enamel, or exposed dentine, the material promotes the growth of crystals in an integrated and organized manner, recovering the architecture of our natural healthy enamel. We have tested the mechanical properties of these regenerated tissues under conditions simulating 'real-life situations' such as tooth brushing, chewing, and exposure to acidic foods, and found that the regenerated enamel behaves just like healthy enamel."

These findings suggest that the gel could eventually offer a way to restore the strength and protective function of damaged enamel rather than simply slowing further deterioration. However, the laboratory results do not yet establish how well the treatment will perform over extended periods in patients.

A New Era of Tooth Enamel Repair?

Beyond its ability to regenerate enamel, the researchers emphasize that the technology was developed with practical dental applications in mind.

The gel is designed to be safe, simple to apply, and suitable for manufacturing on a larger scale. Its versatility could also allow it to be incorporated into several types of dental products, potentially benefiting patients of different ages with enamel erosion, tooth sensitivity, or other problems involving exposed dentin.

Professor Alvaro Mata, Chair in Biomedical Engineering & Biomaterials at the University of Nottingham, led the study and highlighted the potential for translating the discovery into products that dentists can use.

"We are very excited because the technology has been designed with the clinician and patient in mind. It is safe, can be easily and rapidly applied, and it is scalable. Also, the technology is versatile, which opens the opportunity to be translated into multiple types of products to help patients of all ages suffering from a variety of dental problems associated with loss of enamel and exposed dentine. We have started this process with our start-up company Mintech-Bio and hope to have a first product out by next year; this innovation could soon be helping patients worldwide."

The researchers have already begun working toward commercialization through their company, Mintech-Bio, with the goal of introducing an initial product as early as the year following the announcement.

Although further development and clinical validation will be important before the technology becomes an established dental treatment, its ability to recreate the structure and strength of natural enamel represents a promising advance.

If the approach proves successful in patients, it could fundamentally change how dentists address enamel loss, opening the possibility of rebuilding tooth surfaces that previously could only be protected or restored using conventional dental materials.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in dental health: a new gel that can regrow tooth enamel, which has broad implications for preventing tooth decay and sensitivity affecting nearly half the global population. The technology offers a practical, scalable treatment that could transform dental care by restoring natural enamel structure and strength, representing a meaningful positive impact on public health.

articles.title: Opportunistically Detecting Signs of Hypertension on a Consumer Smartwatch
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 05 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11336-3Opportunistically Detecting Signs of Hypertension on a Consumer Smartwatch
articles.content: Hypertension is a silent killer, with over half of affected adults unaware of their condition1,2. This lack of awareness is a major concern, as early intervention is critical for preventing major adverse cardiovascular events3,4. Here we show that applying artificial intelligence (AI) to multimodal waveforms (photoplethysmography and accelerometry) recorded using a widely available consumer smartwatch (AI-PPG-ACC-HTN), without any cuff calibration, can detect hypertension with accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuffed blood pressure (BP) devices in the existing clinical framework. We validated AI-PPG-ACC-HTN in a prospective, multicenter study of 196 diverse participants free from known cardiovascular disease and antihypertensive medication against gold-standard 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring. Over seven days of real-world monitoring, AI-PPG-ACC-HTN detected hypertension with a sensitivity of 65.8% (95% CI, 54.0%-76.3%), specificity of 90.0% (95% CI, 83.2%-94.7%), and positive predictive value (PPV) of 80.6% (95% CI, 68.6%-89.6%). In comparison, initial office BP screening achieved a sensitivity of 55.3% (95% CI, 43.4%-66.7%), specificity of 90.0% (95% CI, 83.2%-94.7%) and PPV of 77.8% (95% CI, 64.4%-88.0%). These results highlight an opportunity for consumer smartwatches to facilitate population-level opportunistic hypertension screening by prompting at-risk individuals toward clinical assessment and confirmatory diagnosis using established cuff-based methodologies, offering an accessible tool to address this major public health challenge.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant health breakthrough where AI applied to consumer smartwatches can detect hypertension with accuracy comparable to traditional methods. This technology offers broad public health benefits by enabling accessible, population-level screening and early intervention for a major silent health risk, supported by a well-designed multicenter study.
articles.personality_title: Smartwatches use AI to spot high blood pressure without cuffs
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – High blood pressure, or hypertension, is a common condition that many people do not know they have. It can cause serious health problems if left untreated. Usually, blood pressure is measured using a cuff device at a doctor’s office or with special monitors.

**What happened** – Researchers developed a new method that uses artificial intelligence (AI) to detect signs of hypertension by analyzing signals from a regular consumer smartwatch. This method looks at light and motion data collected by the watch without needing a blood pressure cuff. They tested this on 196 people over seven days and compared the results to a gold-standard 24-hour blood pressure monitor.

**Impact** – The AI method detected hypertension nearly as well as traditional cuff devices. It correctly identified 65.8% of people with high blood pressure and had a 90% accuracy in ruling out those without it. This is important because it means smartwatches, which many people already wear, could help find high blood pressure early and encourage people to see a doctor for proper tests.

**What's next step** – The next step is to use this technology more widely to screen large groups of people. Doctors and health systems might start recommending smartwatches as a first step to catch hypertension early. Further studies could also improve the AI to detect other health issues.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new AI method on consumer smartwatches can detect high blood pressure as accurately as traditional cuff devices, offering a simple way to find hidden health risks early.

articles.title: The economic benefits of the covid vaccines may be double what we thought
articles.summary: The global health and economic benefits of the covid-19 vaccines were thought to have reached up to $38 trillion in their first year, but a new analysis suggests $64.3 trillion is a more accurate figure
articles.content:
The global health and economic benefits of the covid-19 vaccines were thought to have reached up to $38 trillion in their first year, but a new analysis suggests $64.3 trillion is a more accurate figure

The covid-19 vaccines were costly to produce, but paid for themselves many times over Paul Christian Gordon / Alamy

The covid-19 vaccines may have provided health and economic benefits worth up to $64.3 trillion in the first year alone – almost double an earlier estimate. Previously, researchers calculated that the $79.4 billion invested in developing covid-19 vaccines saw a return of between $4.8 trillion and $37.9 trillion globally in the first 12 months after their rollout. But now, a reanalysis of the data suggests it is actually between $6.43 trillion and $64.3 trillion.

This means that for every $1 spent on the vaccines’ development, between $59.70 and $809 was gained in that year. “It is great to finally see this research published to demonstrate the enormous health and financial benefits gained from covid-19 vaccines, in comparison to the costs that went into their development and delivery,” says Hallie Benjamin at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine.

The $6.43 trillion figure is based on a cost-effectiveness analysis that is generally used in the health sector and factors in quality of life, while the $64.3 trillion figure is based on a cost-benefit analysis used in the public sector.

Advertisement

Both include data from 173 countries on averted hospitalisations, productivity losses and lives saved. For instance, one of the estimates Benjamin and her colleagues used came from modelling that suggested the vaccines prevented 14 million to 20 million deaths in their first year.

The initial $4.8 trillion and $37.9 trillion figures were released when the research was in a preprint stage, before it had been peer-reviewed. “We made many changes throughout the peer-review process that strengthened the quality of our findings,” says Benjamin.

The researchers originally used the Value of Statistical Life Years, which considers how many years a person would be likely to live because of the vaccine, a figure that would be lower if someone was older. As part of the peer-review process, they were advised to use the Value of Statistical Life. Team member Mark Jit at New York University says this treats life spans more equally and is aligned with recommendations for valuing mortality-risk reductions.

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

The cost-benefit analysis figure also increased significantly due to a change from calculating the economic value of avoiding a death, says Jit.

But the returns weren’t equally distributed. The researchers found that the vaccines had the highest returns in richer countries. This was probably because poorer countries accessed them later, so fewer lives were saved and fewer productivity and healthcare costs were averted, says Jit. The results are “a message about the need for being able to distribute the vaccines fairly to the people most in need around the world”, he says.

Richard Carpiano at the University of California, Riverside, says we already knew the covid-19 vaccines were a “life-saving success”, but this study reinforces that “protecting the public’s health is protecting the economy”.

This challenges the “black-and-white” thinking during the covid-19 pandemic on the trade-off between protecting public health through lockdowns and protecting the economy, says Carpiano.

He also hopes these understandings will be used for future infectious outbreaks, or pandemics. “We are in a historical period that has been labelled as ‘a new pandemic age’,” says Carpiano. “The probability of another pandemic in the next 10 years is significant, as are the chances of smaller regional disease outbreaks from existing or new pathogens.” This analysis is “fundamental” to informing policy-making decisions, he says.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant and well-substantiated analysis showing that COVID-19 vaccines provided enormous global health and economic benefits, far exceeding initial estimates. This has broad positive implications for public health policy, pandemic preparedness, and economic recovery worldwide. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights measurable benefits including lives saved and economic returns, making it genuinely inspiring and hopeful.
articles.personality_title: New study shows covid-19 vaccines brought up to $64 trillion in benefits in first year
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Early in the covid-19 pandemic, vaccines were developed quickly but cost billions of dollars. Experts wanted to understand if the money spent on making these vaccines was worth it in terms of health and economic benefits.

**What happened** – A new study reanalyzed data from 173 countries and found the covid-19 vaccines brought between $6.43 trillion and $64.3 trillion in benefits during their first year. This is almost double earlier estimates. The study looked at how many lives were saved, hospital visits avoided, and work productivity maintained thanks to the vaccines.

**Impact** – The findings show that for every $1 spent on vaccine development, countries gained between $59.70 and $809 in benefits. This proves that vaccines not only saved millions of lives but also helped economies recover faster. The study also points out that richer countries saw bigger benefits because they got vaccines earlier, highlighting the need for fair vaccine distribution worldwide.

**What's next step** – Researchers hope this new understanding will guide governments and health groups in planning for future pandemics. Knowing how valuable vaccines are can help make better decisions about investing in health tools and sharing them fairly across all countries.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Covid-19 vaccines saved millions of lives and returned far more money than they cost, showing their huge value for both health and the economy worldwide.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle étude montre que les vaccins covid-19 ont apporté jusqu'à 64 000 milliards de dollars de bénéfices la première année
articles.personality_presentation_fr:

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Une nouvelle étude a réanalysé des données de 173 pays et a trouvé que les vaccins covid-19 ont apporté entre 6,43 billions et 64,3 billions de dollars de bénéfices durant leur première année. C’est presque le double des estimations précédentes. L’étude a examiné combien de vies ont été sauvées, de visites à l’hôpital évitées et de productivité au travail maintenue grâce aux vaccins.

**Impact** – Les résultats montrent que pour chaque dollar dépensé pour développer les vaccins, les pays ont gagné entre 59,70 $ et 809 $ en bénéfices. L’étude souligne aussi que les pays riches ont eu plus de bénéfices car ils ont reçu les vaccins plus tôt, ce qui montre l’importance d’une distribution équitable des vaccins dans le monde.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs espèrent que cette nouvelle compréhension aidera les gouvernements et les organisations de santé à mieux préparer les futures pandémies. Savoir à quel point les vaccins sont précieux peut aider à mieux investir dans les outils de santé et à les partager équitablement entre tous les pays.

**Message clé en une phrase** – Les vaccins covid-19 ont sauvé des millions de vies et rapporté bien plus d’argent qu’ils n’en ont coûté, montrant leur grande valeur pour la santé et l’économie dans le monde entier.

articles.title: Two new Ebola vaccines to join DR Congo clinical trial
articles.summary: Two new Ebola vaccine candidates will be added to a clinical trial in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) as the country continues to battle a deadly outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus.
articles.content:
The announcement by the UN World Health Organization (WHO) follows the recommendation of its independent Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccines Prioritization.

This will mark the first time that vaccines specifically designed for Bundibugyo virus will be evaluated during an outbreak of the disease.

“The fact that these vaccines are ready to enter clinical trials is a testament to the power of science and partnership,” said WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.

He stressed that while vaccines alone will not end the outbreak, “they could become a powerful new tool for bringing it under control”.

‘Hope’ as cases mount

The two vaccine candidates are ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India, and mRNA-1469, developed by the American pharmaceutical and biotech company Moderna.

WHO convened the expert group which this week recommended them for further clinical evaluation, based on available evidence.

The DRC has been battling a deadly outbreak of Ebola disease caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus species for nearly six months and it has become the largest in the country’s history. As of 1 November, there were more than 10,500 confirmed cases and 5,126 deaths.

WHO is supporting the Tumaini multi-vaccine trial, named after the Swahili word for “hope”. It was launched on 23 October in the eastern city of Bunia, capital of Ituri province, which remains the epicentre of the outbreak.

The Ervebo vaccine, used to treat the Zaire species of the Ebola virus, is already being tested to determine if it is effective against Bundibugyo species. The two new vaccine candidates will enter the trial following national approvals.

Tumaini is designed to test multiple vaccine candidates within a single trial, using a ring-vaccination approach that focuses on contacts of people with confirmed Ebola Bundibugyo.

WHO and partners pioneered the strategy during the West Africa Ebola outbreak a decade ago, where a trial in Guinea established the efficacy of the Ervebo vaccine.

Four vaccination rings have been set up and several more are being prepared, while research into other potential treatments is also moving forward.
